title: A new heaven and earth (CCC 1042–1050)

cards: Here's a question a child might ask at a funeral, out loud, where adults keep quiet: what happens to everything else? The trees, the ocean, the dog, the street you grew up on.
All week the Catechism has been talking about people: their callings, their sins, their deaths, their judgment. But the Creed and the Bible don't stop at people.
The last pages of scripture zoom out, to the sky and the ground. Today, the Catechism takes the child's question seriously.

teach.b: This path first read John's vision on day six hundred thirty. Near the end of the Apocalypse, the Book of Revelation, John sees it. In the Douay-Rheims: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth."
And the one on the throne says: "Behold, I make all things new." Not all new things. All things, new.
That small difference is the heart of today. First, creation is waiting.
Saint Paul writes to the Romans that "every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain, even till now," like a woman in labor, waiting to be set free.
At the end of time, the Catechism teaches, the visible universe itself will be transformed, restored to what it was meant to be.
Second, it's renewal, not replacement. Catholic teaching doesn't picture God throwing the old world away and starting over somewhere else.
The universe, the Catechism says, is meant to share in the glory of the risen Christ. Same world, made whole.
Third, the people are part of the picture: the final unity of the human race, God dwelling with people, every tear wiped away. Fourth, the surprise.
Someone might reason that if God will renew everything anyway, there's no reason to look after the earth now. The Catechism says the opposite.

teach.h: HOPE THAT CARES FOR THIS EARTH.
teach.b: Hope for a new earth should make care for this one stronger, not weaker, because what people build in love now is somehow not lost.
Looking back, the week kept getting wider: a Church of many callings, sins forgiven, a soul meeting Christ, the last judgment, and now a whole creation made new.

how: Catholics profess in the Creed their hope for the life of the world to come, and Catholic teaching connects that hope with caring for the earth in the present.

games.q: what does “a new heaven and earth” mean?
o: God renewing all of creation at the end of time
a fresh start for people only, apart from nature
the earth's seasons, made new again each spring

games.q: a new heaven and earth — tap the pairs.
p: behold, I make all things new

s: Catholic teaching says God will scrap this world and start again elsewhere
the Catechism speaks of the visible universe being transformed and restored.
Paul pictures creation groaning, like a woman in labor
"every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain, even till now."
the Catechism says hope for a new earth makes this one matter less
it says that hope should make care for this earth stronger.

games.q: you believe God will one day renew the whole earth. what does that mean for how you treat the earth today?
o: it doesn't matter much, since it'll be renewed anyway
it matters more, since this world is the one being renewed
it's a question for scientists, not faith
games.why: the Catechism says hope for a new earth should not weaken but strengthen care for this one. the world being renewed is this one.

practice: If you can, look out a window, or at one living thing near you: a plant, a tree, a patch of sky. Look at it the way you'd look at something you were going to keep forever: its color, its shape, the way light hits it.
If you pray, thank God for what you see; if you don't, simply let yourself be glad it's there.

wordCard.voice: A new heaven and earth. Catholics believe that at the end of time God will renew the whole of creation, not throw it away, and that this hope calls for care of the earth now. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: all things new. Not thrown away, but made whole. Back tomorrow, same hill.
